Islamic Society of Boston · Est. 1981

A Community’s Journey Across Five Decades

This is the living story of the largest mosque in New England, a community of faith, resilience, and belonging.

About the ISB

Who We Are

A vibrant and engaged American Muslim community

The Islamic Society of Boston (ISB) is a vibrant and engaged American non-profit organization that adheres to Islamic principles. It owns and operates two mosques (masjids): the ISB mosque, located at 204 Prospect Street, Cambridge, Massachusetts, which serves approximately 300 people at weekly Friday prayers (jum’ah); and the ISB Cultural Center (ISBCC), currently the largest mosque in New England, located in the historic inner-city neighborhood of Roxbury, Massachusetts, on 100 Malcolm X Blvd.

The ISBCC serves approximately 1,700 congregants at Friday prayers each week. On major Islamic holidays (Eids), in collaboration with multiple other local mosques, ISB holds multiple sessions to accommodate approximately 10,000 worshipers. The ISB also owns residential property as part of its endowment (waqf). For preserving the Cambridge property’s original architecture, the ISB won the Preservation Award from the Cambridge Historical Commission in 2023.

ISB’s Mission & Vision

ISB’s vision is to build a community of leaders rooted in the Islamic tradition, committed to American ideals, and empowered to serve the common good. A diverse and substantial number of Muslims in Massachusetts helped establish and develop the ISB organization so it can fulfil its mission to teach and live Islam in America.

The journey, stop by stop

  • Quincy, 1964 The Islamic Center of New England opens, the region’s first dedicated mosque. Students later travel there by train and bus to pray.
  • Cambridge, 1995 The ISB’s first mosque opens at 204 Prospect Street and quickly fills.
  • Roxbury, 2009 The ISB Cultural Center opens at 100 Malcolm X Blvd, the largest mosque in New England.
  • Boston, 2026 The ISBCC is named one of Boston’s Historical Markers for the nation’s 250th anniversary.

1981 – 2000

Origins

Origins of the Islamic Society of Boston (ISB)

Beginning with the Immigration & Nationality Act of 1965, passed by Congress, a new wave of students and professionals from more than fifty (50) Muslim countries came to America to work and study in cities like Boston and Cambridge. To preserve their religious identity, Muslim international students and professionals traveled a long distance by train and bus to the suburb of Quincy, where Lebanese Americans had built the first dedicated mosque, the Islamic Center of New England (1964). They contributed their extensive knowledge of Islam and taught religion and Qur’anic Arabic at the Sunday school and also served on the Board of Directors.

ISB’s Mosque in Cambridge

As the decades passed, the international graduate students and their families established their Muslim-American identity in other cities and suburbs across the state. In 1982 a core group of students officially incorporated a non-profit organization, the Islamic Society of Boston. In 1993 they purchased the Knights of Columbus building at 204 Prospect Street, Cambridge Massachusetts. In 1995, after completing renovations, the first mosque in Cambridge officially opened for prayers and was quickly filled with the growing Cambridge Muslim community.

1988 – 2000

Roxbury Vision

An abandoned lot. A sacred duty.

A similar story of growth was taking place in Boston. The Muslim Council of Boston (MCB), a non-profit organization, was incorporated in 1988 by Boston’s African American Muslim leaders, Imam Al-Hajj Abdul Zahir Dawud Ahmad, Yusuf Abdul Hakim, Imam Taalib Mahdi, and Imam Abdullah Taalib Faaruuq. These leaders had seen their two historic, community mosques in Boston and Dorchester reach capacity, and envisioned building a new mosque to encourage greater spiritual and cultural development of Boston’s Muslim community.

In 1989, the MCB successfully acquired a parcel (Parcel R-14) of abandoned land in Roxbury, an area of predominantly African American neighborhoods affected by urban blight and other issues. The land was part of the larger Boston Redevelopment Authority (BRA) redevelopment plan, led by the late Muhammad Ali-Salaam, the BRA’s Deputy Director of Community Planning and Special Projects.

Even with their efforts to raise the millions of dollars needed to build a mosque, by 1998, Parcel R-14 remained undeveloped, and the MCB was at risk of losing the land. As the Cambridge Mosque was steadily outgrowing its facilities, the MCB and Muhammed Ali-Salaam approached the ISB leaders and other members of the Islamic Council of New England (incorporated in 1984), an organization with approximately 20 member mosques at the time, to help raise the necessary funds.

Muslims have always held to the traditional view that acquiring land and constructing a mosque are sacred duties involving faith, patient perseverance (sabr), and prayer. When approached by the MCB, the ISB’s leadership regarded the request as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to address the fast-growing Muslim population in Boston and Cambridge and provide adequate worship space and educational facilities. In August 2000, the BRA approved the final redesignation of the land to the ISB non-profit organization, along with some minor planning modifications and obligations.

2000 – 2009

Adversity

The post-9/11 years of opposition

Following the heinous attacks of September 11, 2001, and the immediate national atmosphere of suspicion of Muslims, the ISB leadership, made up of Muslim graduate students and their families from more than 30 countries, became the targets of Islamophobic attacks from some vocal quarters. The Islamophobic group, consisting of self-proclaimed experts on radical Islam and Islamic terrorism, was joined by media outlets and reporters to embroil the ISB leadership in multiple lawsuits (2003 to 2007), which led to the suspension of construction on the abandoned land (Parcel R-14). See details: The Journey of Faith & Resilience.

In 2005, the ISB organization launched a nine-point countersuit against 17 defendants, including eight media entities and civil conspirators. The countersuit claimed that the plaintiff had engaged in intentional, reckless, and/or negligent reporting and the defamation and intimidation of its leadership. In 2007, following a negotiated legal settlement, all legal cases were dropped. The ISB declared it a legal victory for religious freedom.

Despite the atmosphere of intolerance, the ISB’s building project in Roxbury enjoyed widespread community support. Boston’s Mayor Thomas Menino, the city’s longest-serving mayor, and other prominent and respected figures recognized that the cultural center would serve the needs of the rapidly growing Muslim population in the Greater Boston area. Supporters of the project were also aware that for decades, the MCB and ISB leaders had been promoting increased understanding of Islam in the community through interfaith dialogue.

2004 – 2007

Construction

Raising the Minaret

By 2007, after two decades, the Muslim communities of Greater Boston and New England rejoiced at the Minaret Capping Ceremony of its landmark mosque in Roxbury.

Over 2,500 Muslims gathered outside the mosque to pray, while other members of the Boston community came to share in the joyous occasion.

A 5,000-pound copper canopy (supported by the American flag) was hoisted by a crane and lowered onto the 140-foot-high minaret, and the ISB’s Imam called the faithful to prayer (the athan). This momentous occasion paved the way for continued construction.

In September 2008, the ISB leadership selected the MAS Boston chapter of the Muslim American Society to manage newly built ISB Cultural Center operations and fundraising for a five-year term, with a possibility for an additional five-year term. At the time, MAS Boston was the largest grassroots Muslim organization in Massachusetts, with a dedicated membership base statewide and a network of over 50 chapters nationwide. Their ten-year collaboration (2008–2018) enabled the ISB Cultural Center to deliver the moderate, peaceful message of Islam in Greater Boston and helped each organization expand its reach and impact.
